Axios Future of Defense
By Colin Demarest · Sep 02, 2026

Welcome to September, the official start of Defense Conference Season™️.

  • What's your favorite event? Least favorite? Where should I head next?

🎁 Situational awareness: American Rheinmetall yesterday said it delivered to the U.S. Army its first Lynx XM30 prototype. More of the combat vehicles will be handed over this year.

Up for grabs: Dan Driscoll's exit, the multibillion-dollar Achilles Shield and BWXT's plans for Fort Campbell.

Today's newsletter is 1,837 words, a 7-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: Flummoxed by F/A-XX
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios
 

August came and went, and still no contract for the U.S. Navy's futuristic fighter, F/A-XX, was announced.

Why it matters: The date keeps slipping — inspiring memes, leaving defense industry giants in public limbo, pressuring the service's existing fleet and reminding military watchers of the Trump administration's warplane priority.

Driving the news: Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle in April told reporters the F/A-XX builder would be selected in August. It's now Sept. 2.

  • A CNO spokesperson told me yesterday there was no "additional information to provide on the F/A-XX program or its timing at this point."
  • Aviation Week on Aug. 22 reported that the Navy was "still hopeful an announcement will be made," but noted that it was "out of the service's hands."

State of play: Boeing and Northrop Grumman, the sixth- and fourth-largest defense contractors in the world, have been quietly competing for the contract. (Lockheed Martin, the world's largest, exited a while ago.)

  • F/A-XX is meant to succeed the Super Hornet, long relied upon and recently employed across the Middle East.
  • Boeing and Northrop have expressed to me confidence in their designs and setups. Both companies referred my inquiries this week to the Navy.

Between the lines: Boeing previously won the Air Force's Next Generation Air Dominance fighter competition and is building the sixth-generation F-47.

  • Trump 2.0 has elevated that aircraft — named in part for the 47th president — and has maintained that industry can't handle both endeavors at the same time.

Yes, but: Steve Parker, the Boeing Defense, Space and Security chief executive, this summer pushed back on that narrative ahead of the Farnborough International Airshow.

  • "When we bid what is now the F-47 program and the F/A-XX program, we bid them knowing we had to be able to execute them both," he told reporters in London.
  • "We're excited for the decision; we'll see which way it goes," he added. "Not sure the time frame, but we'll be ready."

Follow the money: The White House's $1.5 trillion budget blueprint for fiscal 2027 included $140 million for F/A-XX.

2. Driscoll dips
 

U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll aboard a Black Hawk helicopter at Fort Stewart, Georgia. Photo: Colin Demarest
 

U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned this week, spurred in part by feelings that his modernization initiatives were being blocked.

Why it matters: The service will soon be without Senate-confirmed leadership, both civilian and uniformed.

The big picture: Driscoll is the latest high-profile exit at the Pentagon.

  • More than a dozen defense officials have abruptly left or been forced out under Trump 2.0.
  • They include Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George, Army Vice Chief of Staff Gen. James Mingus, Navy Secretary John Phelan, Southern Command boss Adm. Alvin Holsey and Defense Intelligence Agency head Lt. Gen. Jeffrey Kruse.

Between the lines: Driscoll resigned amid much media speculation about his rising star, his icy relationship with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the potential protections afforded to him by Vice President JD Vance, a law school classmate.

Zoom in: Driscoll had recently expressed concerns about the state of the Army to President Trump, according to a defense official. (A White House official separately said Driscoll was asked to stick around until after the midterms.)

Zoom out: Both Driscoll and George were advocates of the Army Transformation Initiative, which set out to combine Futures and Training and Doctrine commands and cut big-name weaponry, including the AH-64D Apache, M10 Booker and Gray Eagle drone.

  • "Complacency right now is going to be rewarded with failure and death in the short- to medium-term," Driscoll told me last summer, after visiting Fort Stewart, Georgia.
  • "We should be held accountable if we're not willing to look at everything."

The bottom line: One person clued into the situation described it to me simply: "Sad."

Go deeper: Expect more "reshuffling" in Army's transformation
 
 
3. Exclusive: Aitan emerges
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Aitan today emerged from stealth, backed by tens of millions of dollars and, by its own tally, hundreds of thousands of hours operating alongside the Israel Defense Forces.

Why it matters: The startup is offering "robotic sovereignty as a service" and "edge AI weapon systems" — giving governments and militaries a backbone to build out their unmanned and autonomous forces quickly and with the lessons of the Middle East and Eastern Europe already digested.

  • "Warfare has totally transformed over the past few years," co-founder Daniel Almog told me.
  • "In robotics, the adversary is constantly adapting. The radio-frequency environment is adapting, countermeasures changing. Even the batteries are decaying."

Driving the news: Aitan's reveal coincides with a $41 million funding round led by Deep33 and Dell Technologies Capital. The startup, based in New Jersey, has raised $54 million in equity to date.

  • "We believe physical AI will be one of the most important technology shifts of the coming decade. But first, we need to solve the challenge of coordinating highly complex autonomous systems in challenging real-world environments," Yair Snir, managing director at Dell Technologies Capital, said in a statement to Axios.
  • "They recognized early on that the future of defense belongs to intelligent networks of disparate systems operating together."

Follow the money: Aitan has secured contracts abroad for command-and-control networks and robotic weapon designs.

  • "A lot of countries look for battle-tested systems," co-founder Udi Oster told me. There is, he added, general "skepticism of systems that haven't actually been used in battle."

Context: Both Almog and Oster served in the IDF's Unit 8200, known for intelligence and cyberspace operations.

  • The startup is named in honor of Oster's younger brother, Eitan, who was killed in combat while serving with the Egoz commando unit in Lebanon.
  • Almog and Oster told me his death made their mission — building robotic systems that keep troops out of harm's way — deeply personal.

What's next: Aitan is expanding its team in the U.S. and eyeing European and Asian markets.

4. Shields up
 

Hellenic Air Force F-16s fly over the Parthenon and Acropolis in March 2025. Photo: Theophile Bloudanis/AFP via Getty Images
 

Israel will build Greece a missile-and-drone defense network similar to its own.

Why it matters: The arrangement, dubbed Achilles Shield, is valued at around €3 billion, or almost $3.5 billion. It's billed as the largest defense export in the history of Israel-Greece relations.

Driving the news: The deal was signed Monday in Tel Aviv. It includes:

  • David's Sling, Spyder and Barak MX air-defense systems from Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries;
  • Multi-mission radars from Elta Systems, a subsidiary of IAI;
  • And a new command-and-control system, to be developed by Rafael.

What they're saying: The two countries "share common strategic interests and face shared regional challenges" and plan to "deepen defense cooperation," Israel's defense minister, Israel Katz, said in a statement.

  • He visited Greece a few months ago.

Zoom out: Greece is overhauling its military and stimulating its domestic defense industry in an effort known as Agenda 2030.

  • More than a dozen Greek firms are participating in Achilles Shield, according to the government.

5. ICYMI: Antares action
 

A lead Antares technician welds a component for the company's power conversion system in Torrance, California. Photo: Courtesy of Antares
 

The U.S. Army and Defense Innovation Unit selected Antares to build and operate nuclear microreactors at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, chief executive Jordan Bramble told me.

Why it matters: The military's sky-high energy demand — for reusable batteries, computer farms, radars, housing, weapons and more — is an ideal pressure test for nuclear, which has mounted a comeback in recent years.

Driving the news: The arrangement with Antares is one of a handful announced under the Janus program, the Army's closely watched, multibillion-dollar answer to a White House executive order issued last year.

  • Antares is expected to deliver its reactors in "three packs," according to the service.

What they're saying: "I think the military, for the last decade or so, has been between a rock and a hard place on energy. Most military services bifurcate how they think about energy," Bramble said.

  • "We need to bring more of an operational energy mindset to our installations, here inside the U.S.," he added.
  • "We need to be able to sustain our most critical operations without the grid, without a civilian supply chain, and nuclear power is actually the best thing we have, in terms of capacity factor, to go do that."

Context: Fort Bragg is home to the XVIII Airborne Corps as well as Army special operations and Western Hemisphere commands. Tens of thousands of people, uniformed and civilian, are at the post.

Read the full story here. More on Janus below ⤵️
 
 
6. Quick hits
 

A conceptual look at a BWXT Advanced Nuclear Reactor, or BANR. Photo: Courtesy of BWXT
 

☢️ BWXT's experience with the U.S. Army's Pele project will inform its Janus work at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, where the company is expected to build and operate BANR, a high-temperature, gas-cooled nuclear reactor that uses tri-structural isotropic fuel, Joe Miller, president of government operations, told me.

  • Why it matters: A quick turnaround is expected. Groundbreaking could happen as soon as 2028, with reactor operations kicking off in the early 2030s.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: How much do y'all know about Pele? Worth a deep dive? Let me know!

🔥 Firehawk went 6-for-6 in live-fire testing of Hydra-70 rockets at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona. The rockets were fired from an M261 launcher, seen aboard Apache, Black Hawk and Viper helicopters.

  • Why it matters: "America and its allies need additional production capacity," CEO Will Edwards said in a statement. "And they need modern manufacturing approaches that can bring that capacity online faster."
  • 💭 My thought bubble: The firing footage is worth a watch. Check that out, here.

🌊 Regent Craft, the Seaglider developer, raised $240 million, a mix of equity and debt. The Series B was co-led by Mare Liberum and AE Ventures. Debt capital was provided by Erebor Bank.

  • Why it matters: "This investment marks a critical inflection point for Regent as we move from development into production," CEO Billy Thalheimer said in a statement.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: Yes, Palmer Luckey's Erebor Bank.

🏧 The U.S. Air Force awarded $766 million in contracts for B-52 Stratofortress upgrades on Aug. 25. RTX secured a deal for new AN/APQ-188 radars, while Boeing secured a deal for bomb rack modernization system kits.

  • Why it matters: Big money. Big plane. Big lifespan.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: Michael Marrow at Breaking Defense has much more detail, here.
 
 
7. Check this out
 

Splash one. Photo: Colin Demarest/Axios
 

Here's a drone, with an arm broken and a rotor snapped.

  • It was intercepted by a 9 Mothers 12-gauge turret during Sandhills experimentation at Fort Bragg, North Carolina.

Why it matters: I ran out of room for this photo last week.

What they're saying: Asked about metrics of success, 9 Mothers chief executive Russell Smith told reporters at the range: "It's how many drones we kill before they cross over us."
